title: A Democratic Sweep Is Priced In. A Surprise Isn't.
summary: A look at the midterm outcomes and what markets are pricing
body_markdown:
A look at the midterm outcomes and what markets are pricing


**IN TODAY'S ISSUE**


-


**A Democratic sweep is predicted, but elections have been notoriously hard to predict.** Prediction markets have all but settled next Tuesday's midterms, with Democrats heavily favored to take the House and more likely than not to take the Senate. However, confident election forecasts have a long record of being wrong.


-


**Election outcomes matter for digital asset policy.** A non-consensus outcome would matter for crypto, mostly through who chairs the committees that write and oversee digital asset policy, and whether the industry's most active legislators keep their seats.


-


**Non-consensus outcomes are cheap via options.** BTC options price only a modest Election Day move, and longer-dated volatility sits near record lows. For investors who disagree with the consensus, expressing that view has rarely cost less.


## The Market Has Already Called the Election


The crypto industry is still absorbing the impact of the Binance hack, and the full picture has yet to emerge. But the U.S. election calendar keeps moving, with Election Day on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The midterm elections will determine the makeup of Congress for the next two years and shape lawmaking, budgets, and committee leadership. And while the votes are yet to be fully cast, let alone counted, prediction markets have pretty much settled winners and losers.


Polymarket gives Democrats a 91.5% chance of winning the House and a 66.5% chance of winning the Senate, with a Democratic sweep of both chambers priced at the same 66.5%. The House has been a more consistent call, with Democrats favored throughout the past year. The Senate, however, is a different story. A year ago, Polymarket gave Democrats roughly a 24% chance of taking the chamber, and the odds were still below 50% at the end of July. Most of the move came after August, which makes the current consensus recent.


Consensus Outcome is Knock on Crypto


The read-through for crypto has been mostly negative. Market structure legislation remains stalled in the Senate, and a Democratic Congress would likely shift its attention from passing digital asset rules to one of antagonism. The other part of the consensus outcome is gridlock. With President Trump holding the veto through January 2029 and the Senate filibuster still in place, a Democratic Congress could pass bills but not get them signed, while the White House could not get its agenda through committees run by the other party. Most new legislation, in either direction, would stall. Markets appear to have drawn the conclusion, which is that the election will not change very much, and priced it accordingly.


## Confident Favorites Have a Habit of Losing


The problem with consensus election forecasts is that elections don’t always go as predicted. Here’s a brief look at several outcomes that were confidently misjudged. On the day of the 2016 Brexit referendum, betting markets put the odds of a Remain victory at about 92%. Months later, The New York Times’ Upshot gave Hillary Clinton an 84% chance of winning the presidency. The day before Australia’s 2019 federal election, bettors gave Labor about an 87% chance of victory, but the Coalition won. On the eve of the 2022 U.S. midterms, PredictIt (prediction market) gave Republicans a 72% chance of taking the Senate, but Democrats held on to control.


The most recent example is the freshest. Polymarket had Flávio Bolsonaro as the favorite in Brazil's presidential race from mid-September, peaking at 89% after he led the first round. The day before the October 25 runoff, he was still at 77%. Lula won 51.8% to 48.2%.


This doesn’t mean prediction markets or polls are useless. The point is more limited. A candidate with a 66.5% chance of winning should lose about one time in three, and the factors behind an upset can affect several races at once. If polls systematically miss in one close Senate race, they may miss in others too. That makes the range of possible outcomes wider than any single headline probability might suggest.


## Crypto's Legislators Are on the Ballot Too


For crypto, the outcome depends on a handful of specific races as much as on overall control. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown is favored at 67.5% to return to the Senate against Jon Husted. Brown is a former Senate Banking Committee chair and a longtime critic of the industry, and his seniority could put him in line to chair the Senate Agriculture Committee, which shares jurisdiction over the CFTC's role in digital assets. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas, who voted for both the CLARITY and GENIUS Acts in the House, is a 90% favorite for an open seat. Iowa's open seat leans toward Ashley Hinson at 55.5%, though both she and Josh Turek have backed crypto legislation. In Nebraska, Senate Banking member Pete Ricketts is a 71.5% favorite against an independent challenger.


The House is where the risk to crypto's legislative bench is most visible. French Hill, who chairs the House Financial Services Committee, is a solid favorite at 81%. Bryan Steil, who leads the committee's digital assets subcommittee, is at 53%, essentially a coin flip. Bill Huizenga, a CLARITY cosponsor, is the underdog at 44%. Steven Horsford, a Democrat who introduced the PARITY Act, is safe at 96%. Even before control of the chamber is decided, two of the three Republicans most involved in writing crypto bills face a real chance of losing their seats. In a Republican House, that would cost the industry two of its most experienced authors. In a Democratic one, it would compound the loss of committee control.


## Oversight Replaces Legislation Under a Democratic Congress


Committee chairs set the agenda, and the likely changes are significant. If Democrats take the Senate, Elizabeth Warren would be in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee. Industry participants expect her to use subpoena power aggressively, with the OCC's approval of national trust charters for crypto firms, including Ripple, Coinbase, and the Trump-family-linked World Liberty Financial, an obvious early target. On the House side, Maxine Waters had been expected to reclaim the top seat on Financial Services if Democrats win, but she now faces challenges from Sean Casten and Bill Foster. Casten is widely seen as the most aggressive of the three on crypto oversight.


Hostile legislation would still need the president's signature, which makes anything introduced to become law. The GENIUS Act is already on the books. The SEC, CFTC, and OCC can continue writing rules within their existing authority, regardless of who is in charge of Congress. We think the more realistic risk from a Democratic Congress is a steady stream of hearings, investigations, and headline noise rather than new restrictions. For traditional investors, the same committees oversee banks, stablecoins that compete with deposits, tokenized securities, and fintech charters, and government funding fights tend to grow more contentious under divided government.


## Options Are Pricing a One-Day Event


BTC options show the election clearly, but they confine it to a narrow window. On Deribit, at-the-money implied volatility for the November 1 expiry, the last before Election Day, sits at 30.7%. The November 6 expiry, the first to include the vote, jumps to 37.8%, a 7.1 point step. Backing out the extra variance in that window implies an Election Day move of roughly ±3.5% for one standard deviation, about twice what options price for an ordinary day.


Past elections have moved BTC well outside that range. From the close on Election Day to the close the following day, measured by the CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate at 4pm ET, BTC rose 2.2% in 2020, fell 8.9% in 2022, and rose 9.4% in 2024. The 2022 decline coincided with the collapse of FTX and says more about that episode than the midterms. Even so, two of the last three elections produced moves of roughly 2.5 to 3 times what options currently price. This is not a claim that options always underprice elections. Ahead of the 2024 vote, they priced a move of roughly 7% to 8% and were close. The point is that the market is now pricing less than half of what it priced, and got, two years ago.


The timing of the premium also matters. In 2024, the gap between one-week and one-month implied volatility sat around 2 points a week before the election, then widened to 27 points on Election Day before vanishing the next session. This year, the same gap stood at 1.1 points seven days out, broadly tracking 2024's early path. History suggests the event premium builds late and disappears quickly, which implies that positioning ahead of the final days has tended to be cheaper than positioning on the eve of the vote. It also means an option bought for the event pays only if BTC actually moves, since the extra implied volatility evaporates once the result is known.


## BTC Volatility Is Near Record Lows While Other Markets Brace


Outside the election week, bitcoin options are about as inexpensive as they have ever been. Six-month at-the-money implied volatility set a record low of 37.3% on October 5 and sits in the 0.8th percentile of


readings since 2019. A year ago, the same measure was 45.7%.


Bitcoin’s calm stands out against other markets. The MOVE index of Treasury volatility sits near 98, in the 89th percentile of the past year, after jumping in late September as the 10-year Treasury yield reached a 19-year high above 5.1% on strong manufacturing data, oil above $90, and rising expectations of a Fed hike, even as the FOMC stands pat. The VIX, at 17.5, is unremarkable, in the 58th percentile. Bitcoin one-month implied volatility is in the 25th percentile and six-month in the 6th. Bitcoin options are also priced at about 2 times the VIX, compared with a typical ratio of about 2.8 times since 2019. Rates markets are pricing uncertainty, equity markets are pricing roughly the usual amount, and BTC is pricing very little.


One caveat deserves mention. BTC's realized volatility has been lower still, with 30-day realized volatility near 24.8%, so options are not cheap relative to how BTC has traded in recent weeks. Our interpretation is that recent calm is a weak guide to an event with a record of surprising forecasters, and that the more relevant comparison is with BTC's own history and with the size of past election reactions.


## What the Market Has Priced, and What It Hasn’t


The consensus is clear and, by most measures, reasonable. Democrats are favored to win the House and have the better odds in the Senate, gridlock is the likely result, and the near-term legislative outlook for crypto is subdued. Both the election odds and the options market reflect that view. BTC implied volatility near record lows, options are pricing a narrower range of outcomes than past elections have produced. Less reflected is the chance the consensus is wrong, whether through a Republican hold of the Senate, a larger Democratic wave, or the loss of key crypto legislators in the House. Election forecasts have missed before, sometimes badly. The market has already voted. The electorate hasn’t.
